title: Developing a Departmental Approach to Problem-Solving
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the fourth post of his departmental-support series, Craig Barton argues that most maths lessons are a diet of fluency practice and diagnoses why: it is easier to plan and deliver, hides gaps in subject knowledge, feels safer for a Head of Department, and is what students expect. He uses Colin Foster's two-tunnel image to define problem-solving as travel into the unknown. He dismisses end-of-topic problem lessons and problems buried on slide 63 as solutions that rarely reach most students. Richer task types are ideal but hard to implement, so he proposes a smaller step: one short problem in every lesson, with a fixed routine for the thirty-second silence, mini-whiteboards, and paired talk. Three classroom examples show the approach working, including with a disengaged Year 11 class.
points: Fluency practice dominates because it is easier to plan, easier to deliver and safer for departments with non-specialists, not because anyone thinks it is enough.
A diet of nothing but fluency leaves students unable to cope with twists in exam questions and teaches them to see maths as disconnected algorithms.
Barton rejects end-of-topic problem lessons and problems tucked at the end of the scheme of work, because many classes and students never reach them.
His alternative is deliberately modest: one short problem in each lesson, with at least ten minutes reserved and a fixed routine of silent thought, mini-whiteboard notes and paired discussion.
CPD for the approach has colleagues solve the problem as mathematicians for five minutes and then reflect on pedagogy, since either step alone misses the point.
quotes: But at a more fundamental level, problem-solving is what maths is - or at least should be - all about. We learn procedures so we can do interesting things with those procedures.
This is problem-solving. The path to the solution may be short or long, but the key point is it is not immediately obvious what we need to do.

At a deeper level, if all students experience is fluency practice, they start to view maths as a series of disconnected algorithms they must remember and carry out with no real purpose, and promptly switch off from the subject.
Fluency practice is easier to plan. You can grab a bunch of questions from a number of sources and use them in lessons without needing to do much preparation beforehand.
Fluency practice can help disguise a lack of subject knowledge. Armed with a set of questions and - crucially - a set of answers, most teachers can get through the lesson.

Another approach I see is to include challenging, problem-solving-type questions or tasks on slide 63 of an epic PowerPoint, or tucked away in Column M on the Excel version of the scheme or work. The issue here is that few classes and few students ever get to this point, and therefore whole cohorts of students may never experience anything above and beyond fluency practice.

Where possible, we should aim to leave at least 10 minutes of the lesson to do the problem-solving activity. This stops problem-solving from being ignored completely, or shoved in during the last 30 seconds, preventing many students from engaging with it.
